evidence.snippet: San Telmo is the oldest surviving neighborhood in Buenos Aires, Argentina. With its atmospheric cobblestone streets, gas lamps, and crumbling colonial mansions, it serves as the heartbeat of the city's early history.

evidence.source: A Brief History of San Telmo
evidence.snippet: The Early Days: Originally named Alto de San Pedro, the area began as a high ground where Spanish settlers and indigenous people interacted. Some historians believe Pedro de Mendoza may have made his first, short-lived founding attempt of Buenos Aires nearby around 1536.
evidence.title: A Brief History of San Telmo
evidence.contextHeading: A Brief History of San Telmo

evidence.source: A Brief History of San Telmo
evidence.snippet: Colonial Era & Saladero: During the 17th and 18th centuries, it became an outlying district inhabited by salted-meat producers (saladeros), tanners, and brickmakers, alongside African slaves who lived along the southern fringes.
evidence.title: A Brief History of San Telmo
evidence.contextHeading: A Brief History of San Telmo

evidence.source: A Brief History of San Telmo
evidence.snippet: The 1871 Yellow Fever Epidemic: San Telmo was once an upscale residential address for wealthy aristocratic families who built grand Italianate mansions. However, the catastrophic yellow fever outbreak of 1871 forced wealthy residents to flee north to neighborhoods like Recoleta and Palermo. They left behind their grand homes, which were subsequently subdivided into conventillos (tenement housing) for incoming European immigrants, or left abandoned.
evidence.title: A Brief History of San Telmo
evidence.contextHeading: A Brief History of San Telmo

evidence.source: A Brief History of San Telmo
evidence.snippet: Cultural Rebirth: The influx of immigrants, combined with working-class roots, helped foster early tango culture, local bohemian artistry, and community life that defines the neighborhood today.

evidence.source: stayviax.com
evidence.snippet: San Telmo is the oldest neighbourhood in Buenos Aires, and its cobblestone streets hold enough history to fill several lifetimes. On this self-guided walking tour, you'll trace how sailors, slaves, immigrants, and tango singers turned a muddy colonial outpost into the soul of the city. You'll also discover how a yellow fever epidemic, two British invasions, and millions of Italian immigrants each left their mark on this single neighbourhood. The tour starts at Basílica de San Francisco, where a time capsule is hidden inside a stone statue on the facade. From there, you'll walk south along Defensa Street, passing the oldest pharmacy in Buenos Aires and the spot where residents repelled two British invasions from rooftops using stones and boiling water. You'll also hear how that resistance helped spark Argentina's independence movement, and why the street you're walking is named after those events.
evidence.title: Two to Tango: A San Telmo Self Guided Walking Tour

evidence.source: www.guruwalk.com
evidence.snippet: San Telmo is one of the most historic neighborhoods in Buenos Aires: its cobblestones have witnessed much of the city, and its old mansions — abandoned after the yellow fever of 1871 — have become patios for tango and art. I invite you to explore it with me, from the possible founding site to the corner where Mafalda was born. What we will discover:Parque Lezama: the green lung of the neighborhood and possible cradle of the first Buenos Aires (1536)Russian Orthodox Church: its blue domes, a piece of St. Petersburg in the heart of San TelmoSan Telmo Market and Pasaje Defensa: iron and glass from 1880, artists and traditional eateriesPlaza Dorrego and Defensa Street: where tango was born in the patiosPaseo de la Historieta: a stop to meet Mafalda And as always, we share some mate along the way to chat about our identity (remember to request it free of charge 2 hours in advance, so I arrive fully prepared).Why this tour?I am Gabriel, a history teacher and journalist. I have been teaching this for over 30 years, and my idea is simple: to move away from the generic tour and propose a real conversation, entering the patios where this culture was forged. Small groups, no rush.Important info: Meeting point: Monument to Don Pedro de Mendoza (Av. Brasil and Defensa) We start on time Bring cash: many artisans at the fair do not accept cards Upon booking, you receive my real-time location via WhatsApp and a complimentary PDF guide\"San Telmo is not visited, it is felt.\"
evidence.title: SAN TELMO: The stories beneath the cobblestones.

evidence.source: www.expedia.com
evidence.snippet: Discover Buenos Aires' passionate soul and faded grandeur with your self-guided audio tour, allowing you to explore Argentina's intoxicating capital at your own pace. Begin in the elegant Plaza de Mayo where the Casa Rosada's pink facade has witnessed Eva Perón's speeches, military coups, and the Mothers who still march for their disappeared children. Wander through the boulevards of Recoleta where mansions and the famous cemetery housing Evita's tomb. Cross into the colorful streets of La Boca where tango was born in the conventillos of Italian immigrants and the painted zinc houses of Caminito create Buenos Aires' most photographed scene. Explore the cobblestoned streets of San Telmo where Sunday antiques markets, crumbling colonial architecture, and intimate milongas preserve the Buenos Aires of memory and imagination. Discover the transformed Puerto Madero waterfront, then lose yourself in the bookshops of Corrientes Avenue that stay open until midnight.
evidence.title: Découvrir Buenos Aires : Une visite autonome

evidence.source: www.tripshock.com
evidence.snippet: Behind just 2.30 meters of facade, Casa Mínima is the narrowest house in Buenos Aires, preserving the oldest myths and traditions of San Telmo. From the times of slavery to the origins of tango, this visit to the narrowest house in Buenos Aires reveals the stories that shaped the neighborhood's identity. The visit takes in Casa Mínima and the adjacent space on the corner of the block.
